analogy.p: Think of an ecosystem as a city. Producers are the farms and power plants that bring energy in, consumers are the people who use it, and decomposers are the recycling and waste-treatment teams that turn rubbish back into resources. If the recycling teams stop, the city runs out of materials; if a major supplier closes, many other businesses are affected. This shows interdependence and why change spreads through the system. The analogy breaks down because a city has planners who manage it, whereas ecosystems regulate themselves through feeding links and have no controller.
analogy.t: A city and its supply network

bullets: Define an **ecosystem** and give examples at **small (pond), medium and global (biome)** scales.
Describe **producers, consumers (primary, secondary, tertiary) and decomposers**, and give an example of each.
Draw and interpret **food chains and food webs**, with arrows showing the direction of energy flow.
Explain **nutrient cycling** using stores (biomass, litter, soil) and transfers.
Explain **interdependence** and how a change (such as removing a species) has knock-on effects.
Describe the **global distribution of biomes** and link it to climate (temperature and rainfall).
Know a **small-scale UK ecosystem** with detail: biotic and abiotic parts, links, and the effect of change.
core.h: What the specification asks you to know
core.p: AQA Geography 8035 (The living world) asks you to know an overview of the **distribution and importance of ecosystems at different scales**, from a small local ecosystem to a global biome. You must understand the **concept of an ecosystem**: its **producers, consumers and decomposers**, **food chains and food webs**, **nutrient cycling**, and the **interdependence of climate, water, soils, plants, animals and humans**. You also need to know how a **change in one component affects others**, and you must study **a small-scale UK ecosystem as a case study** (for example a freshwater pond, woodland, heathland or sand dune). It matters because ecosystems are the basis of the whole topic and 4, 6 and 9 mark questions use food webs and case-study detail.

bullets: **Biotic** = living: plants, animals, fungi, bacteria.
**Abiotic** = non-living: sunlight, temperature, water, rock, soil type, pH, oxygen, nutrients, wind.
**Scales**: small (pond, rotting log), medium (woodland), global (biome such as the tropical rainforest biome).
An ecosystem is a **system**: inputs (sunlight, rain, nutrients from weathering), stores (biomass, soil), transfers (feeding, decomposition), outputs (leaching, run-off, harvest).
The **community** is all the living things; the **habitat** is where an organism lives; a **population** is one species in the habitat.
Ecosystems are **dynamic**: they change over time and respond to disturbance.
Humans are **part of** ecosystems and also change them (farming, building, pollution).
core.h: What is an ecosystem? Scales, biotic and abiotic components
core.p: An **ecosystem** is a community of living things (plants, animals and microorganisms) that interact with each other and with the non-living environment in which they live. The living parts are called **biotic** components and the non-living parts are **abiotic** components. Ecosystems exist at **many scales**: a small-scale ecosystem such as a rotting log, a pond or a hedgerow; a medium-scale one such as a woodland or a lake; and a large-scale ecosystem called a **biome** such as tropical rainforest or tundra. Each is a **system**, which means it has inputs, stores, transfers and outputs. What links all of them is that energy from the Sun is captured by plants and passed through the system.

bullets: **Producers** (autotrophs): algae, pondweed, trees, grass; they capture light energy and store it in **biomass**.
**Primary consumers** (herbivores) eat producers, e.g. water snail, rabbit, caterpillar.
**Secondary consumers** (carnivores or omnivores) eat primary consumers, e.g. dragonfly nymph, frog.
**Tertiary consumers** eat secondary consumers, e.g. heron; an **apex predator** has no natural predators.
**Decomposers**: bacteria and fungi break down dead material and release nutrients.
**Scavengers and detritivores** (earthworms, woodlice) feed on dead matter and speed decomposition.
Photosynthesis in words: carbon dioxide + water, with light energy, makes glucose + oxygen.
Each step in the feeding sequence is a **trophic level**.
core.p: Organisms in an ecosystem have different roles in the flow of energy and nutrients. **Producers** are green plants and algae that make their own food by **photosynthesis**, using sunlight, carbon dioxide and water, so they are the base of every food chain. **Consumers** cannot make their own food and get energy by eating other organisms. **Decomposers** (bacteria and fungi, helped by earthworms and other detritivores) break down dead plants and animals and waste, which **returns nutrients to the soil** so producers can use them again. Without decomposers nutrients would stay locked in dead material and the ecosystem would run down.

bullets: **Arrows point to the consumer** (the direction energy moves), never "eats".
Food chains are **simplified**; food webs are **more realistic** and more stable because species have alternative foods.
Only a small fraction of energy (often around 10 per cent) passes to the next level; the rest is lost as heat through respiration, in waste, and in uneaten parts.
So higher trophic levels have **less biomass and fewer individuals**, which is why there are few top predators.
**Biomass** is the total mass of living organisms.
To predict changes: if a **predator decreases** its prey tend to **increase**; if prey **decrease**, the predator also tends to decrease (less food).
Use **link words**: "so", "because", "as a result" to chain the effects through the web.
Remember that the **producers** are the base and all energy ultimately comes from the **Sun**.
core.p: A **food chain** shows a single path of feeding and energy transfer, for example algae to water snail to frog to heron. Real ecosystems are more complex, because most animals eat several things and are eaten by several predators, so we draw a **food web** made of many linked food chains. In both, the **arrows show the direction of energy flow**, so they point from the organism that is eaten to the organism that eats it. A food web shows **interdependence**: a change in the number of one species changes others. At each step much of the energy is **lost** (as heat from respiration, movement, and in waste and uneaten parts), so there is less energy available at higher levels, which is why food chains are short and top predators are fewer in number.

bullets: Three stores: **biomass**, **litter**, **soil**.
Transfers: **leaf fall / death** (biomass to litter), **decomposition** (litter to soil), **uptake by roots** (soil to biomass).
Inputs: **weathering** of rock and **precipitation** (rain deposits nutrients); also nutrients added by humans as fertiliser.
Outputs: **leaching** (nutrients washed down through the soil) and **surface run-off**; also removal by **harvesting** crops.
Warm, wet conditions speed **decomposition**, so litter is quickly broken down; in cold places litter builds up because decomposers are slow.
In the tropical rainforest most nutrients are in the **biomass** and litter is small, whereas in cold places the largest store is the litter.
Removing vegetation (deforestation) cuts the transfer back to the soil and increases leaching, so the soil becomes infertile.
It is a **closed-looking cycle with inputs and outputs**, so it is a system.
core.p: Nutrients such as nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium are taken up by plants from the soil, passed along food chains, and returned to the soil when organisms die or produce waste. This is **nutrient cycling**, and a standard way to show it is a diagram with three **stores**: **biomass** (living material), **litter** (dead leaves and fallen material on the ground) and **soil**. Arrows between the stores show **transfers**, and the size of an arrow represents how much nutrient is moved. **Inputs** come from weathering of rock and from rainfall, and **outputs** leave through leaching and run-off. Decomposers drive the litter-to-soil transfer, so rapid decomposition (as in warm, wet places) means fast cycling.

bullets: **Climate to plants**: more warmth, light and rain gives faster growth; very dry or cold climates limit plants.
**Plants to soil**: leaf litter adds humus (organic matter), roots hold soil together and reduce erosion.
**Soil to plants**: nutrients and water storage determine which species can grow.
**Plants to animals**: provide food and habitat; animals pollinate and spread seeds.
**Animals to soil**: waste and dead bodies add nutrients; burrowing mixes and aerates the soil.
**Humans** can disrupt every link: drainage changes water, farming changes soil, pollution affects wildlife, and carbon emissions change climate.
This web of links is why ecosystems are **fragile**: a single large change can cause a chain reaction.
core.h: Interdependence: climate, water, soils, plants, animals and humans
core.p: The components of an ecosystem are **interdependent**, meaning each one relies on and affects the others. **Climate** (temperature, sunlight and rainfall) controls which plants can grow and how fast. **Water** supplies plants and shapes soil. **Soils** supply nutrients and support roots and are formed from rock and dead organic matter. **Plants** feed animals and return organic matter to the soil, and animals spread seeds, graze plants and add waste to the soil. **Humans** change all of these through farming, building, pollution and the burning of fossil fuels, which changes climate. Because of these links a change to one part spreads through the whole system.

bullets: **Balance** = populations roughly constant over time because feeding, growth and loss are matched.
**Removing a predator**: prey increase, they eat more producers, producers decline, then the prey run short of food and crash.
**Removing a producer** (for example by pollution): consumers lose their food and decline up the web.
**Adding an invasive species** (for example a plant that shades out native plants): native species lose out and food webs change.
**Higher biodiversity** gives more alternative food sources, so the ecosystem recovers from change more easily.
Changes can be **short term** (a hot summer) or **long term** (climate change).
In exams, trace the change step by step through the web and name the species.
core.h: Balance and the impact of change
core.p: A healthy ecosystem is in a state of **balance** (equilibrium), where populations stay roughly steady because feeding, growth and loss are matched. Change can upset this. Natural changes include disease, drought, fire and the arrival of a new species. Human changes include habitat loss, pollution, overfishing, introducing **invasive species** and climate change. The effects spread through the food web. If a **producer** declines, the primary consumers lose food and their predators decline in turn. If a **top predator** is removed, its prey may increase and overgraze the producers, which damages the ecosystem. This is why scientists say ecosystems need **biodiversity** (a wide variety of species) to be stable.

bullets: **Tropical rainforest**: near the equator (roughly 0 to 10 degrees); hot all year, rain all year; very high biodiversity.
**Savanna**: either side of the rainforest (roughly 5 to 20 degrees); hot with distinct wet and dry seasons; grasses and scattered trees.
**Hot desert**: around 15 to 35 degrees; very low rainfall; sparse, specially adapted plants.
**Temperate deciduous forest**: mid-latitudes (about 35 to 60 degrees); mild, with rain all year and four seasons; trees lose leaves in winter.
**Taiga**: high northern latitudes (about 50 to 65 degrees); long cold winters, short summers; coniferous trees.
**Tundra**: very cold, near the poles (above about 65 degrees); permafrost; low-growing plants.
The boundaries are **approximate** and gradual, and **altitude** can create tundra-like conditions on high mountains even near the equator.
Climate controls vegetation, vegetation controls animals, and together they shape the soil: a clear example of interdependence.
core.p: A **biome** is a large-scale ecosystem covering a huge area with similar climate, vegetation and animals. The world's main biomes include **tropical rainforest**, **savanna (tropical grassland)**, **hot desert**, **temperate deciduous forest**, **taiga (coniferous forest)** and **tundra**. Their distribution is mainly controlled by **climate**, especially **temperature and rainfall**, which vary with **latitude** (distance from the equator). Heating from the Sun is strongest at the equator and weaker towards the poles, and global air circulation creates wet areas near the equator and dry areas around 30 degrees north and south. Altitude, distance from the sea and ocean currents also modify the pattern.

bullets: **Abiotic factors**: sunlight (needed for photosynthesis, limited by depth and algae), water temperature (changes with season), dissolved oxygen, pH, depth, nutrient levels from soil and rain.
**Producers**: algae (phytoplankton), pondweed, water lilies and reeds at the edge.
**Primary consumers**: water snails, mayfly nymphs, tadpoles, water fleas.
**Secondary consumers**: dragonfly nymphs, diving beetles, sticklebacks, adult frogs.
**Tertiary consumer / top predator**: heron (visits the pond).
**Decomposers**: bacteria and fungi in the mud break down dead plants and animals.
Pond **zones**: edge plants, floating plants, submerged plants and the bottom mud, each with different organisms.
Fieldwork could use **nets for pond dipping**, quadrats for edge plants, and probes to measure temperature, oxygen and pH.
core.h: Small-scale UK ecosystem case study: a freshwater pond
core.p: For the small-scale UK ecosystem you need to know a **specific example** with real detail. This note uses a **UK freshwater pond** (for example a village or school pond); your school may have studied a woodland, heathland or sand dune, in which case use the same structure with your own details. A pond is a small, self-contained ecosystem with clearly defined edges, which makes the links easy to see. The pond is in a temperate climate, so it has warm summers, cold winters and rain all year. The living things depend on the abiotic conditions such as light, temperature, oxygen, depth and nutrient levels.

bullets: Example food chain: **pondweed to water snail to frog to heron**.
Example food chain: **algae to mayfly nymph to dragonfly nymph to stickleback to heron**.
Energy flow: arrows point from **eaten to eater** (pondweed to snail).
Nutrient cycle: **dead leaves and animals (litter on the mud)** are decomposed by bacteria and fungi, nutrients dissolve in the water and are taken up by plants.
Interdependence: more fish eat more insect nymphs; fewer nymphs means more algae-eaters survive, which can reduce algae.
The heron's droppings and the leaves from nearby trees carry nutrients **into** the pond (inputs); outflow carries them out.
The more different species, the **more stable** the pond (higher biodiversity).
core.h: The pond food web and nutrient links
core.p: In the pond, the **algae and pondweed** use sunlight to make food and form the base of the web. Snails and mayfly nymphs graze them, and tadpoles feed on algae and plant material. These herbivores are eaten by dragonfly nymphs, sticklebacks and frogs, which in turn are eaten by the heron. The web has several connections, so if one food source declines the consumers can switch to another. When organisms die, **decomposers** break down their bodies and leaves that fall in, releasing nutrients to the water and mud that producers take up again. Rainwater and run-off from surrounding land add nutrients, and some leave when water flows out or the heron removes fish.

bullets: **Fertiliser run-off** to nutrient enrichment to algal bloom to light blocked to plants die to decomposers use oxygen to animals die (eutrophication).
**Drought or hot summer**: lower water levels, higher temperature, less dissolved oxygen (warm water holds less oxygen).
**Removing sticklebacks or dragonfly nymphs**: prey such as mayfly nymphs and tadpoles increase, then they overgraze algae and plants and may run out of food.
**Invasive plants** reduce biodiversity and native species lose habitat.
**Human pressure**: litter, trampling of margins, and dumped fish upset the balance.
**Management**: leave a buffer strip of vegetation around the pond, avoid fertiliser, remove invasive plants, and keep the pond partly shaded and varied in depth.
**Overall effect**: the food web is simplified, biodiversity falls, and the pond becomes less stable.
core.h: Impact of change on the pond ecosystem
core.p: The pond is sensitive to change because it is small. A major issue is **nutrient enrichment**: fertiliser or sewage run-off adds nitrates and phosphates, which causes an **algal bloom**. The bloom blocks sunlight, so submerged plants die. Bacteria decompose the dead material and use up the **oxygen** in the water, so fish and invertebrates suffocate; this process is called **eutrophication**. Other changes include a **drought** (the pond shrinks and warms), removal of the top predator (fish or amphibian numbers change), **invasive species** such as New Zealand pigmyweed that covers the surface and shades out other plants, and people adding fish or dumping rubbish.

bullets: Ecosystem **services**: provisioning (food, water), regulating (climate, flooding), cultural (recreation, education).
Always **name** species and conditions: "algae", "mayfly nymph", "dissolved oxygen", not "plants" and "animals".
Link terms: **producer, consumer, decomposer, biotic, abiotic, interdependence, balance**.
Use **cause and effect chains** of at least three steps.
Mention both **natural and human** causes of change.
Show **scale awareness**: small ecosystems change quickly; biomes are large and slower to change.
End with a judgement such as "the pond is vulnerable because it is small and a change in one species affects many others".
core.h: Why ecosystems matter to people and how to use the case study
core.p: Ecosystems provide humans with **ecosystem services**: food, water, raw materials, flood protection, climate regulation (carbon storage), recreation and wildlife value. A pond, for example, supports wildlife, helps store and clean water, and gives people a place for learning and relaxation. The key examination skill is to use the case study **with specific detail** rather than general statements: name organisms, abiotic factors, links and the causes and effects of change. In extended answers show the chain of consequences clearly and finish with a judgement about how sensitive or resilient the ecosystem is.

exam: Command words: **describe** = state features; **explain** = give reasons using "because"; **suggest** = apply knowledge to an unfamiliar food web; **assess** = judge using evidence.
1 mark: a correct term (producer, decomposer, biotic). 2 marks: a statement plus a reason or development.
Food web questions: write the **sequence of effects** using linking words; 3 to 4 marks usually need at least three linked steps.
Always say "arrows show the **direction of energy flow**" when asked about a diagram.
Nutrient cycle diagrams: label **stores** (biomass, litter, soil), **transfers**, inputs (weathering, rain) and outputs (leaching, run-off).
Case study (4 to 6 marks): quote **named species**, abiotic factors and the effects of a **specific change**; vague answers stay in the lower levels.
Distribution questions: link to **climate**, giving temperature and rainfall for the biome, and refer to latitude.
Model phrase: "If the heron population declined, sticklebacks and frogs would increase, so there would be more feeding on mayfly nymphs, and fewer nymphs would graze the algae."
Use percentage change in data questions: change divided by original multiplied by 100, showing working.
Graph or map questions: quote values and units, and describe the pattern (anomalies too).
Avoid "animals die because there is no oxygen" without the **sequence**: bloom, light blocked, plants die, decomposers use oxygen.

mistakes.r: Arrows show energy flow, so they point from the organism that is eaten to the one that eats it.
mistakes.w: Drawing food web arrows from the eater to the food.

mistakes.r: Plants are producers that make food by photosynthesis using light energy, carbon dioxide and water.
mistakes.w: Saying "plants are consumers" or "plants eat sunlight".

mistakes.r: Biotic is living; abiotic is non-living (for example temperature, light, pH).
They break down dead matter and release nutrients back to the soil or water for producers to reuse.
mistakes.w: "Decomposers just get rid of dead things."

mistakes.r: Energy is not destroyed; it is lost as heat from respiration and in waste and uneaten parts, so less is available at the next level.
Name species, abiotic factors and links, and state causes and effects in detail.
mistakes.w: Using general statements for the case study ("the pond has animals").

mistakes.r: Trace the effect step by step through the food web and explain why each step happens.
mistakes.w: Only describing the change, not the knock-on effects.

mistakes.r: Latitude controls temperature and rainfall, but altitude, ocean currents and distance from the sea also affect distribution.
mistakes.w: Saying biomes are only decided by latitude.

mistakes.r: Name the three stores (biomass, litter, soil) and the transfers, inputs and outputs.
mistakes.w: Describing nutrient cycling without naming stores and transfers.

summary: The specification asks you to know how ecosystems work (producers, consumers, decomposers, food chains and webs, nutrient cycling and interdependence), how they are distributed as biomes, and to study a small-scale UK ecosystem such as a pond in detail, including the impact of change. It matters because food web reasoning and case-study detail are tested in 4, 6 and 9 mark questions.

terms.d: A community of living organisms that interact with each other and with their non-living environment.
The living components of an ecosystem, such as plants, animals and microorganisms.
The non-living components of an ecosystem, such as sunlight, temperature, water, soil and pH.
An organism, such as a green plant or algae, that makes its own food by photosynthesis.
An organism that gets its energy by eating other organisms (primary, secondary and tertiary).
An organism, such as bacteria or fungi, that breaks down dead material and returns nutrients to the soil.
A single sequence showing which organism eats which and the direction of energy transfer.
A diagram of many interconnected food chains in an ecosystem.
The position of an organism in a food chain.
The total mass of living organisms; also a store in the nutrient cycle.
The transfer of nutrients between the stores of biomass, litter and soil in an ecosystem.
Dead leaves and other organic material on the ground, one store in the nutrient cycle.
The way that living and non-living parts of an ecosystem rely on one another.
The variety of living species in an area.
A large-scale ecosystem with similar climate, vegetation and animals, for example tropical rainforest.
Nutrient enrichment of water that causes an algal bloom, oxygen depletion and the death of aquatic life.
A non-native species that spreads and harms native species and ecosystems.
The washing of nutrients down through the soil by water.

worked.q: The population of mayfly nymphs in a pond falls from 250 per square metre to 100 per square metre after fertiliser run-off. Calculate the percentage change. (2 marks)

worked.ans: 10 per cent transferred; the rest is lost as heat from respiration, and in waste and uneaten parts, so less energy reaches higher trophic levels.
worked.q: The producers in a food chain store 10 000 kJ of energy in a year. The primary consumers store 1 000 kJ. Calculate the percentage of energy transferred and suggest two reasons why the rest is not transferred. (3 marks)
steps: Energy is lost as heat through respiration.
Energy is lost in waste and in parts that are not eaten (such as roots or bones).

worked.ans: Model answer: Fertiliser run-off adds nutrients which cause an algal bloom. The bloom blocks light so pondweed dies. Bacteria decomposing the dead plants use up oxygen, so animals such as sticklebacks and nymphs die, and the food web is simplified and biodiversity falls.
worked.q: Explain how fertiliser run-off from nearby fields could affect the animals in a UK pond. (4 marks)
steps: Fertiliser adds nitrates and phosphates (nutrients) to the water.
Algae grow rapidly (algal bloom) and block sunlight, so submerged plants cannot photosynthesise and die.
Decomposers break down the dead plants and use up dissolved oxygen.
Animals such as fish and mayfly nymphs suffocate, so numbers fall and the food web is simplified.
